system.name: OctoCache
system.one_liner: a caching layer on top of OctoMap that speeds up voxel updates in 3D occupancy mapping for autonomous systems

components.name: Voxel batch
components.role: incoming batch of voxel updates to be applied to the map

components.name: Cache
components.role: flattened, table-based cache that handles all voxel updates before they reach the octree

components.name: Evicted
components.role: voxels evicted from the cache, reordered by Morton code before updating the tree

components.name: Octree
components.role: OctoMap's underlying octree data structure, updated from evicted cache entries

flows.what: write update to a tree node, ordered by Morton code

content.key_idea: OctoCache inserts a flattened table-based cache in front of OctoMap's octree so most voxel updates hit the cache, and only evicted, Morton-code-ordered voxels reach the costlier octree.
content.reading_order: Left to right: Voxel batch writes into the Cache; evicted entries are reordered and written into the Octree; the right panel lists the resulting speedup numbers.

summary: OctoCache is a caching layer built on top of OctoMap that accelerates voxel updates in 3D occupancy mapping for autonomous systems such as UAVs. This overview figure shows the OctoCache System on the left: a Voxel batch is written into a flattened, table-based Cache instead of going straight to the octree; evicted cache entries are reordered by their Morton code before being written to the underlying Octree, cutting the number of costly tree memory accesses. The OctoCache Performance panel on the right lists the resulting headline numbers: OctoCache is up to 5.85x faster than the octree thanks to over 95% cache hit rates, its overall mapping generation is 46-88% faster than plain OctoMap, and an OctoCache-based UAV navigation system saves up to 28% of flight time. The figure pairs a compact blue/orange pipeline diagram with concrete speedup callouts rather than a detailed architecture breakdown.

notes: The performance numbers (5.85x, 46-88%, 28%) are read directly from the callout text in the image; they are consistent with the abstract's reported speedups (45.63%-88.01%, 28% flight-time reduction) though phrased slightly differently there.
